shared_text:
The flight. A twin-engine airliner descending towards a busy airport in visual conditions.

The crew. The first officer was the pilot flying and the captain the pilot monitoring.

What happened. Based on the latest recorded airport information, the crew had planned for an approach to one runway. Air traffic control instead assigned a charted visual approach to a different runway, and the crew changed to it. Between two fixes on the visual approach, the first officer was following the vertical path guidance from the flight management system while configuring the aircraft for landing. At about this time, air traffic control told the crew that they had received a low altitude alert for the aircraft. The captain then took control of the aircraft.
safe_outcome: The captain flew the rest of the approach and landed the aircraft. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was crossing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
bracket_fill: [climbing / descending / crossing] = crossing; [this aircraft] = this aircraft
notes: UNDER THE 150-WORD MINIMUM. The report has a single three-sentence narrative and the shared text uses every fact in it; reaching 150 words would need invented detail, so it was left short for James to decide (keep short, or replace the case). Removed under rule 3: the first officer's lesson to confirm flight management system altitudes independently and not be rushed into an amended approach. Because of that removal, the shared text does not say the approach change was late or that the flight management system altitudes were wrong; neither is stated as fact in the narrative. Moved under rule 5: the captain landing the aircraft. Removed under rule 6: the airport, runway numbers, the named visual approach and fix names. Judgement calls: (1) the aircraft type is not reported, so twin-engine airliner is used; (2) the local-time band (afternoon, in January) could include dusk, so day or night is not stated; (3) the 'FMS snowflake' is rendered as the vertical path guidance from the flight management system; (4) the synopsis says the aircraft descended below terrain minimums, but the narrative says only that air traffic control reported an altitude alert, so the shared text keeps to the narrative; (5) the coded results (air traffic control assistance, a new clearance, the crew requesting clarification) are not used because their order is unknown. Bracket: 'crossing', because the deviation was low on a visual approach near a busy airport, where the plausible conflict is lower traffic crossing the approach path. | DECISION by Claude, 1 Oct (deviation D5): kept at 122 words. The report is three sentences and padding is not allowed.
